claims.text: Repeatedly alternating layers create a high density of chemically distinct interfaces.
Repeatedly alternating layers create a high density of crystallographically distinct interfaces.
Interfaces in high-entropy-alloy multilayer coatings act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Interface-mediated obstruction of dislocations retards creep and plastic flow.
The proposed coatings contain alternating compositional layers with well-defined interfaces.
Reducing interlayer spacing increases interface density when coating thickness is held constant.
Interfaces between dissimilar layers produce lattice mismatch and chemical heterogeneity.
Lattice-mismatched and chemically heterogeneous interfaces serve as dislocation-pinning sites.
Differences in crystal structure across interfaces hinder dislocation motion.
Differences in chemical composition across interfaces hinder dislocation motion.
Interfacial pinning prevents continuous dislocation glide under sustained load.
Preventing continuous dislocation glide reduces time-dependent plastic deformation relative to a uniform microstructure.
Multilayer coatings with higher interface densities will accumulate less creep strain than homogeneous coatings under otherwise identical conditions.
The beneficial interface effect is expected to be prominent under moderate-to-high stress and temperature where creep is activated.
The creep-resistance benefit may diminish when stress or temperature exceeds the regime in which interfaces remain stable or effective dislocation barriers.
Very coarse layer spacing may limit the beneficial effect.
Compromised interfacial integrity may limit the beneficial effect.
